measurement.happened: The dominant story of the week in Singapore was the Nvidia chip scandal and its fallout. Multiple outlets reported that Nvidia had been using Singapore as a key routing point for AI chips destined for China, and that the company had stopped disclosing its Singapore sales figures even as its total revenues hit 104 billion dollars. The Financial Times ran a detailed piece on how Jensen Huang's family had shaped Nvidia's Singapore dealings, suggesting personal and business ties went deeper than a simple distribution hub. Singapore's Prime Minister Wong publicly acknowledged that the new US chip curbs would have 'some impact' on the city-state. Singapore then moved to seek what it called 'trusted access' to AI chips under the new US restrictions, and Reuters reported that Singapore and the US agreed to keep discussing a framework called Megaspeed while scrutiny of the Nvidia scandal widened. Bloomberg noted that crowded Singapore bank stocks faced rotation as AI risks mounted, signalling that the financial sector was feeling the tremors. In short, Singapore found itself at the center of a US-China chip tug-of-war, and the government was in active damage control mode, trying to preserve its position as a trusted intermediary without looking like it was helping China dodge restrictions. The second major theme was the Indonesian wildfire haze. Indonesia's President Prabowo formally apologized to Singapore and Malaysia for the smog that had been drifting across the region. The apology was reported by Reuters, Bloomberg, and Al Jazeera on November 15 and 16. However, Deutsche Welle reported on November 20 that the forest fires were still spewing smoky haze over Singapore and Malaysia, meaning the problem was not yet fully resolved despite the diplomatic gesture. Singaporeans continued to deal with degraded air quality, and the episode reinforced the perennial tension between Singapore and its larger neighbor over transboundary pollution. The third theme was Singapore's broader financial and business activity. Bloomberg reported that Singapore-based DayOne paused its US IPO plans citing data center and market concerns, a sign that the tech-fintech funding window may be narrowing. On a positive note, Singapore's property market saw sales hit a year-high, and the sovereign wealth fund teamed with Saudi Telecom to bid for a UK data center stake. Quantitative trading firm Graviton expanded its offices in both Singapore and India, and a Singapore profit surge minted two new Indian billionaires. India's Paytm partnered with Singapore's Funding Societies in a deal worth up to 21 million dollars, and NETS deepened its partnership with Ant International around agentic commerce and mobile payments. Singapore also urged deeper ASEAN ties in AI and energy as it prepares to take the ASEAN chair in 2027, signaling its ambition to lead regional digital and energy policy. In the cybersecurity space, SentinelOne and Singapore's Digital and Intelligence Service announced a partnership to strengthen cyber defense and advance secure AI, a notable signal that the government is investing in next-generation digital security. The US Treasury separately pressed Singapore and Malaysia on Iran sanctions compliance, suggesting that Singapore's role as a global financial hub is under closer regulatory watch, particularly regarding how transactions linked to Iran flow through its banks. On the sports front, Singapore hosted a football event that ended in humiliation: Brazil crushed the local side 7-0, with Vinicius Jr scoring a first-half hat-trick. The match was covered by Reuters, AP, and Al Jazeera. Earlier in the week, Japan had stunned Brazil 3-2 in Singapore in another match, suggesting this was some kind of friendly tournament or exhibition series. The WTA Singapore Open tennis tournament was also underway, with the BBC tracking scores and schedules. In aviation, a Singapore Airlines jet had to U-turn after a second cabin smoke incident, raising fresh questions about safety protocols. A smaller cultural note: AFP profiled the opening of Moutai House in Singapore, a Chinese baijiu brand's cultural and retail presence in the city. An Indian driver also won a 1.3 million dollar lottery prize in Singapore, a feel-good story that made the BBC. Overall, the week was defined by Singapore's central but uncomfortable role in the US-China tech rivalry, the ongoing haze nuisance from Indonesia, and a busy undercurrent of financial deals, sports, and institutional partnerships.

crystal.eli5:
Think of Singapore like a tiny, super-smart middleman sitting between two very big, very powerful friends who are arguing. One friend (the US) wants to make sure the other friend (China) does not get too many fancy computer chips. Singapore has been helping the chips get from one friend to the other, and now everyone is asking: 'Are you sure you are not helping the other friend cheat?' So next week, Singapore is going to sit down with the US and try to write a rulebook that says, 'Here is how we can keep trading chips in a fair, trusted way.' It is like two kids arguing over a toy, and the small kid in the middle has to explain why they are allowed to hold the toy.

At the same time, the air is still smoky because of fires in Indonesia. The Indonesian president already said sorry, which is nice, but the smoke has not gone away. So Singaporeans will still be coughing and wearing masks, and the governments will probably have another meeting to figure out how to actually stop the fires, not just apologize for them. It is like your neighbor saying 'Sorry about the smoke' but still not turning off the barbecue.

In the business world, a lot of deals keep happening every week. New companies sign partnerships, new data centers get planned, new payment systems get built. It is like a very busy marketplace where the specific stalls change every week but the market itself is always full of people. One company that wanted to go public in the US paused its plans, which is a small signal that the funding mood might be cooling. And the property market is doing well, with sales at a yearly high, so people are still buying homes.

Singapore Airlines also had a second weird problem where smoke appeared in a plane's cabin, and the plane had to turn around and land. Two times in a row is a lot, so the airline will probably have to explain what is going on and make sure passengers feel safe. It is like your favorite restaurant having a food-safety issue twice in a week; you want to know they fixed it before you go back.

And there is a tennis tournament happening, and a football match where Singapore lost by a lot. These are smaller stories, but they keep the sports pages busy and give people something to talk about at lunch.
